newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Belgium's 1997 budget attacked for lack of reforms.
newsitem.headline: Belgium's 1997 budget attacked for lack of reforms.

text.p: Belgian newspapers on Wednesday criticised the government for not having used its powers of executive rule to push through more radical reforms in its 1997 budget which was unveiled Tuesday.

"This budget is terribly flat, without imagination, without brilliance, a repetition of previous budget exercises. Was it really neccessary to give special powers to the government and muzzle the parliament for this?" asked Brussels daily Le Soir.
Prime Minister Jean-Luc Dehaene in May asked parliament to be allowed to rule by executive decree for the drafting and execution of the 1997 budget and an overhaul of the social security system.

Parliament in July grudgingly gave the green light for three so-called "framework laws" on the budget, social security and corporate competitiveness. These laws -- also called "special powers" -- allow the Belgian government's decrees to take immediate force of law without prior parliamentary approval.

Dehaene's centre-left cabinet spent the whole summer coming up with an 80 billion Belgian franc ($2.5 billion) austerity package which will cut the public deficit to 2.9 percent of GDP in 1997 from 3.3 in 1996.
Like all the budgets in previous years, this one too was a long list of small tax increases and spending cuts here and there. But again no fundamental reforms were decided.

"The Maastricht target has been reached. But without glory. In this budget there are no traces of measures which will ensure the long-term financing of social security. And we are still trying to understand why Dehaene demanded special powers to draw up a budget like this," said Catholic daily La Libre Belgique.
Flemish liberal opposition daily Het Laatste Nieuws agreed.
"When it suits him, Dehaene sidetracks parliament because he says he needs to work quickly. Then he does not manage to present his budget a day earlier than in previous years."
Francophone financial daily L'Echo too said it was among those that regretted the framework laws. "They really were not necessary and push aside the parliament," it said.
Left-leaning daily De Morgen said that Dehaene's piecemeal approach was at least partly inspired by fear of street protest.
"This budget is not revolutionary...This way Dehaene avoids a French scenario whereby the whole country grinds to a halt because of strike actions," it said.
Flemish Catholic daily De Standaard agreed: "This budget hurts nobody, especialy not those big groups which could organise social protest."
Like all other papers, De Standaard was sharply critical of the patchwork character of the budget, which includes long lists of measures too technical to explain to the layman.

"This budget again includes tricks and 'one shot' measuers. The worst is that the government presents the payment of the pensions of the (state-owned) postal system as a budget saving," said De Standaard.

Several papers also reproached Dehaene of having focused too much on the budget while ignoring the two scandals of political murder and of peadophile kidnap, sex and murder which have traumatised the country since mid-August.
"During that horrible summer, Dehaene was on holiday abroad. During the period of mourning...while confidence in our institutions collapsed, Dehaene withdrew into his budget talks." Le Soir said.
"Even now, at the presentation of his budget, he has adressed himself more to the financial markets and the EU institutions than to the citizens of this country," it added. ($1=31.38 Belgian Franc)
